title: ⭐⭐ Practice: back on yourself, and told what to do

questions.prompt: Emna is checking four sentences she has written in her English notebook. Three of them are correct. In which one has she put a reflexive pronoun where English uses none at all?

options.text: Rania asked herself whether she had read the question properly.
Mouna taught herself to use the new program.
Nizar could not concentrate himself with all that noise.
The two candidates introduced themselves to the examiner.

questions.explanation: "Nizar could not concentrate himself with all that noise." is the sentence to correct: in English the verb concentrate takes no pronoun after it at all, and the line should read Nizar could not concentrate. Your own language builds this verb with a pronoun, and that is exactly why the mistake is so common on a paper. "Rania asked herself whether she had read the question properly." is correct, and the reflexive is compulsory there: the girl who asks the question and the girl who is asked it are one and the same. "Mouna taught herself to use the new program." is correct too, and means that she had no teacher, the reflexive filling the place of the person taught. And "The two candidates introduced themselves to the examiner." is correct as well: they gave their own names, so the doer and the receiver are once again the same people.

questions.prompt: Rania is going through four sentences that all use must. In three of them must says that something has to be done. In the fourth it does something quite different: it says what somebody concludes from what can be seen. Which one is the fourth?

options.text: The office light is on; somebody must be working late.
Candidates must write their name on every sheet they hand in.
Every pupil must be in the yard when the second bell rings.
We must leave the laboratory as we found it.

questions.explanation: "The office light is on; somebody must be working late." is the fourth: nobody is being ordered to work late, and the speaker has no power to order anything. She sees a lit window, and must gives the one explanation that fits what she sees. That is a deduction, and when the thing is already over it becomes must have plus a past participle. "Candidates must write their name on every sheet they hand in." is a plain obligation, the rule of an examination. "Every pupil must be in the yard when the second bell rings." is an obligation as well, and it is the line that catches most candidates out, because must be looks exactly like the deduction: read what the sentence does, never the two words it is built from. And "We must leave the laboratory as we found it." states a duty the speaker takes on with everybody else, which is once again something to be done and not something worked out.

questions.prompt: Mouna is sorting the new words of the theme into two columns. Three of these four say what a candidate herself goes through on the day of the exam. The fourth names an action aimed at a thing, and it belongs to the other lesson of the theme. Which one is the fourth?

options.text: to panic
to fail
to go blank
to suppress

questions.explanation: "to suppress" is the odd one: it means to put an end to something, and it needs somebody who does it and something that is done away with, which is why the uniform lesson uses it of a school accused of suppressing the individuality of its pupils. You suppress a thing — a feeling, a report, whatever makes somebody different — and never a person. "to panic" names a state that comes over a candidate, and nobody panics somebody else. "to fail" is the candidate's own result when she does not reach the mark she needed, not an action aimed at anything outside her. And "to go blank" is said of a mind that suddenly holds nothing at all, which is once again something she lives through rather than something she does to a thing.

questions.prompt: In three of these four sentences the reflexive pronoun can be crossed out and what is left is still a complete sentence. In which one would crossing it out leave a sentence with a hole in it?

options.text: The pupils painted the club room themselves.
Rania cut herself on a sheet of paper.
The head teacher herself opened the meeting.
We carried the boxes upstairs ourselves.

questions.explanation: "Rania cut herself on a sheet of paper." is the sentence that would break: herself is the object of cut, and it names the person the cutting was done to. Take it away and Rania cut on a sheet of paper no longer says what she cut, so the reflexive there is compulsory. In "The pupils painted the club room themselves." the object is already the club room, and themselves only insists that no painter was called in; The pupils painted the club room is still a full and true sentence. "The head teacher herself opened the meeting." shows the same emphatic use in another position, right after the subject, and it can be removed just as easily. And "We carried the boxes upstairs ourselves." again has its object, the boxes, so ourselves adds emphasis and nothing more.

questions.prompt: Hedi borrowed a set of past papers from the school library in June and still has them at home. Nobody has asked for them back, and nothing at all will happen to him if he keeps them another week. Emna reminds him of what a decent person does. Which sentence does she say?

options.text: You needn't take those papers back before the new term.
You had better take those papers back before somebody notices.
You should have taken those papers back at the end of June.
You ought to take those papers back to the library.

questions.explanation: "You ought to take those papers back to the library." is what Emna says: ought to gives advice as a duty, what is right and what is expected of a person, and that is exactly the ground she is standing on. "You needn't take those papers back before the new term." says the opposite of a duty, that the effort can wait, when her whole point is that it should not. "You had better take those papers back before somebody notices." turns the reminder into a warning, and a warning needs something unpleasant waiting at the end of it; the situation says plainly that nothing will happen to Hedi. And "You should have taken those papers back at the end of June." looks back at a date that is gone and blames him for it, which is a reproach and not the reminder of a duty he can still carry out today.

questions.prompt: Emna is copying the useful expressions of the theme onto the last page of her notebook. Three of her four lines are correct English. Which line must she cross out and write again?

options.text: to cope with three hard papers in one day
to fail the written exam by a single mark
to conform the rules of a new school
to check your answers twice

questions.explanation: "to conform the rules of a new school" is the line to cross out: this verb never takes its object straight, so Emna must write to conform to the rules of a new school. English locks conform to its preposition, and letting the to fall is the commonest way of spoiling it. "to cope with three hard papers in one day" is right, and cope holds on to its with in the same way; a candidate copes with a difficulty, never copes a difficulty. "to fail the written exam by a single mark" is right too: when its object is an exam, a test or a subject, fail takes that object with nothing at all between them. And "to check your answers twice" is correct as it stands, since check also takes its object directly, and adding a preposition would break it.
